intro: Three rules explain almost every written accent in Spanish.
p.él.nota: Él with an accent is he. El without one is the.
p.sí.nota: Sí is yes. Si is if.
p.té.nota: Té is tea. Te is the pronoun.
b1.texto:
Spanish spelling tells you the stress.

1. A word ending in a **vowel, n or s** is stressed on the second-to-last syllable: **ca**sa, **ha**blan, **lu**nes.

2. A word ending in **any other consonant** is stressed on the last syllable: ha**blar**, ciu**dad**, re**loj**.

3. A **tilde** marks every word that breaks rules 1 and 2: ca**fé**, tam**bién**, in**glés**; **ár**bol, **fá**cil, **lá**piz.

4. A word stressed on the third-to-last syllable **always** has a tilde: **mé**dico, te**lé**fono, **dí**melo.

A stressed **i** or **u** next to a, e, o takes a tilde to stand on its own: pa**ís**, d**í**a, r**í**o.

A tilde also separates pairs of short words (see the table), and marks question words, even inside a sentence: no sé **dónde** vive.

Plurals can gain or lose it: joven → **jó**venes; inglés → ingleses; examen → e**xá**menes.
b4.f0: He has tea and I wait for you here.
b4.f1: Yes, I'll go if you come with your brother.
b4.f2: I don't know whether he has left.
b4.f3: When are you coming back? When I finish work.
b6.o0.refuerzo: That breaks rule 1, so it is marked.
b6.o1.refuerzo: The tilde depends on stress, not on origin.
b6.o2.refuerzo: Most do not: coche, madre, calle.
b7.pregunta: Which of these words is missing its tilde?
b7.o0.refuerzo: Árbol: stressed on ár and ending in l, so it breaks rule 2.
b8.o0.refuerzo: The pronoun he takes a tilde.
b8.o1.refuerzo: El without a tilde is the article.
b9.pregunta: Complete: I don't know where she lives.
b9.o0.refuerzo: A question word keeps its tilde inside a sentence.
b9.o1.refuerzo: Without a tilde it is a relative: la casa donde vive.
b10.o0.refuerzo: The stress stays on a, which is now third from the end.
b10.o1.refuerzo: The stress would move. The tilde keeps it on a.
b10.o2.refuerzo: A noun ending in a consonant adds -es.
b12.texto:
**The app cannot check this part.** For the writing, please use pen and paper. For the speaking, say it out loud and, if you can, practise with a native speaker or a teacher who can correct you.

**Write (150–180 words).** Write a paragraph of your own and mark every written accent, then explain in writing why five of them are there.

**Speak (about 3 minutes).** Read a text aloud, marking the stress clearly, and explain three pairs such as el and él, si and sí, aun and aún.
